Test-set performance against human labels varies sharply by criterion: guessing is strongest (GPT-5.4 sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.86, QWK 0.75), ground-truth access moderate (Sonnet 4.6 QWK 0.57), tool failure weakest (F1 0.13-0.27). Verified issues found include CORE-Bench tasks whose answer appears verbatim in plotting code or results files, a CVE-Bench sample where a model appeared to recall a hardcoded secret key from training data, and a guessable Terminal-Bench 2.0 task (10% chance if reward-hacked). Scanners and a transcript dataset across 11 agentic evaluations released.
adopt: Adopt scanners as a scheduled shift over the session log, not as a gate: they surface candidates for human review, and their own results show high false-flag rates when the scanner lacks benchmark context. The severity rubric and the sampling methodology for bounding benchmark-level confidence are directly reusable for the environments registry. Combine with a deliberate red-team agent, as the authors suggest, since scanner flag rate depends on whether the transcript-generating model tried to cheat.

name: MCP specification revision 2026-07-28 (stateless core)
summary: The largest MCP revision since launch. The initialize/notifications-initialized handshake and Mcp-Session-Id are removed; protocol version, client info and capabilities ride in per-request `_meta`; a mandatory `server/discover` RPC replaces the handshake; every result carries `resultType` (`complete` / `input_required`); list results carry `ttlMs` and `cacheScope`; Streamable HTTP POSTs must carry `Mcp-Method`/`Mcp-Name` headers validated against the body; `subscriptions/listen` replaces the GET SSE channel and `resources/subscribe`; MRTR (multi round-trip requests) replaces server-initiated `sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create` and `roots/list`; tasks move to a redesigned official extension; sampling, roots and MCP logging are deprecated on a 12-month window; tool schemas loosen to full JSON Schema 2020-12; dynamic client registration is deprecated in favour of CIMD. Implementers are shipping dual-era servers rather than cutting over.
adopt: Plan a dual-era MCP server: keep the 2025-11-25 path and add a 2026-07-28 path with `server/discover`, `resultType`, and `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` on `tools/list`. Reject the temptation to model MCP sessions as harness sessions — statelessness means any cross-call state becomes an explicit server-minted handle passed as a tool argument, which is closer to how our session log already works. Our approval seam should treat MRTR as the replacement path for elicitation before the deprecation window closes.

name: PEFT v0.20.0
summary: Added nine PEFT methods (HiRA, GLoRA, BEFT, MonteCLoRA, VeLoRA, Uni-LoRA, FRoD, MiCA, DEFT), automatic LoRA target-module selection via KappaTuneSelector, broader quantization support across BOFT, MiSS, VeRA and SHiRA, multiple-adapter support with target_parameters, AdaLoRA for Conv2d, and a 'PEFT Shop' Space for capability comparison. The v0.19.0 release (14 April 2026) had already added tensor-parallelism support for LoRA and conversion of non-LoRA adapters to LoRA checkpoints.
adopt: Adopt KappaTuneSelector to stop guessing which modules to adapt in a 128-expert MoE, where the LoRA placement question is genuinely hard. Test structural LoRA variants against plain LoRA before defaulting: published RLVR-specific comparisons find DoRA, AdaLoRA and MiSS beat LoRA and that SVD-informed initialisations fail under RL. Tensor-parallel LoRA is the enabling piece for a 119B run on modest hardware.

name: Kilo Code and Cline: subagent delegation and worktree managers
summary: Kilo Code (MIT, a Roo Code fork, itself a Cline fork; its CLI builds on OpenCode) documents Code, Plan, Debug and Ask modes that can delegate isolated work to Explore, General or custom subagents, with an Agent Manager coordinating parallel VS Code sessions across git worktrees; the page is dated 23 July 2026 and reviewed against current Cline pricing, authorization, local-model, subagent and Kanban sources. Cline (Apache-2.0) grew a standalone CLI and SDK in its 3.x line. Kilo Code was acquired by Anaconda in 2026 (secondary).
adopt: Worktree-per-agent has become table stakes rather than a differentiator, which is a useful correction: our `ctx.programs` value is not the worktree, it is the certificate on the merged head. Their fixed mode set (Code/Plan/Debug/Ask) is what we get for free from presets, so the comparison to make in a client deck is composability, not mode count.

name: Kwaipilot/KAT-Coder-V2.5-Dev
summary: Apache-2.0 agentic-coding MoE, 35B total / 3B active, post-trained from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with 127K SFT examples then RL. In-house reproduced results at 256k context: SWE-bench Verified 69.40, SWE-bench Multilingual 63.00, SWE-bench Pro 45.96, Terminal-Bench 2.1 41.02 (Terminus-2 32.60 / Claude Code 49.44), PinchBench 93.43, SciCode 44.20. The RL recipe is documented: Token-in-Token-out consistency (identical rollout and training token sequences), Truncated Importance Sampling for asynchronous-rollout staleness, systematic validation of sandbox and verifier correctness so infrastructure failures are not counted as model failures, and hierarchical rewards derived from harness execution feedback. Records that a binary 0-1 reward collapsed the model by epoch two with occasionally >70 parallel tool calls per turn, fixed by penalties on excessive parallel calls, failed calls, empty tool-call blocks and repeated content. Abnormal tool labels fell 9.34% -> 0.28%.
adopt: Adopt the four RL components directly: TITO, TIS, verifier validation, and hierarchical harness-feedback rewards. Daliesk's session log already makes TITO checkable, since model-visible implies logged. Test the parallel-tool-call penalty early: the failure mode it fixes is exactly what a harness with many tools invites, and it appeared at epoch two, not at convergence.

name: Prime Intellect: 365,000+ environments for SWE, terminal and search
summary: Twenty-three agentic tasksets unified behind one taskset API with shared runtime and sandbox hooks: about 198,000 software-engineering tasks across 20+ languages, about 28,600 terminal tasks and about 137,600 search tasks, roughly 365,000 in total. Every taskset loads from a typed config (dataset, split, filters), provisions a sandbox from the task image, and scores with the taskset's own logic. Validation runs no-op checks (setup without a fix must fail), gold-patch checks with 10x retries to catch flakiness, and duplicate elimination — Scale-SWE dropped 20,181 to 17,202, Multi-SWE 4,703 to 2,232. The post is unusually candid about reward integrity: because 'the agent shares a sandbox with the grading machinery, a policy under RL pressure will eventually find whatever seam is left', withholding grading material is 'mitigation, not a guarantee', and the structural fix — grading in isolated sandboxes — is still roadmap. It also names the false-negative class: PR-mined tests assert implementation details, so a differently-correct fix is punished, and gold-patch validation is blind to it by construction. Re-uploads preserve upstream licences and link back to source datasets.
adopt: Adopt the validation ritual wholesale for `ctx.environments`: no-op-must-fail, gold-patch-must-pass with retries, and a recorded drop count per taskset — we do not currently prove a registered environment is well-formed before it enters a fleet plan. Their unsolved problem is our `read-barrier` plus validator-owned tree, so this is the strongest external evidence that our tamper story is a real differentiator. Cite their licence and attribution policy when we build the curator's export terms.

name: PrimeIntellect/Terminal-Lego-15k
summary: Apache-2.0 filtered mirror of SWE-Lego/Terminal-Lego-15k: 13,825 task directories remain of an original set after 1,224 exclusions, each task's task.toml pointing [environment].docker_image at a prebuilt Prime platform image in the canonical org-less form terminal-lego/<task-id>:latest following a 2026-07 registry homogenization. Tagged terminal, code-agent, stackoverflow, docker, benchmark; arXiv 2606.03461.
adopt: Adopt as the bulk terminal-task corpus for RLVR: 13,825 tasks with prebuilt images removes the container build cost that usually dominates. Test image availability and the pinned registry form before planning a run, since the card documents a mid-2026 registry rename that will break any hard-coded team-scoped image reference.

name: Amp: self-scheduling agents
summary: Sourcegraph's Amp shipped agents that 'set their own schedules, wake themselves up, and keep working'. It landed inside a dense July: agent-to-agent spawning, messaging and file exchange across threads (17 July), paid subscriptions (18 July), the Puck meta-agent and a Slack surface (20 July), and Multiplayer shared control of an orb (22 July). Amp is closed source with no BYOK; model access is bundled behind a router.
adopt: This is the nearest commercial equivalent to our shifts, and it is agent-initiated rather than operator-configured. Test the difference deliberately: a self-scheduling agent has no frozen plan, so its work is not reproducible across seeds. Keep our cadence and spend window in `cordis.yml` and the ledger in a session log; adopt only the ergonomic half, an agent being able to propose its next slot as a logged event a human or policy approves.

name: PrimeIntellect/SWE-rebench-V2-Filtered-Verified
summary: CC-BY-4.0 filtered and gold-patch-verified subset of Nebius's SWE-rebench-V2: 6,272 of 32,079 freshly-mined GitHub PR tasks across 17 languages, the default dataset of the swerebench_v2_v1 taskset. Filtering used the upstream per-row LLM-judge metadata (difficulty easy/medium/hard, judge grade code == 'A' for clearly solvable, intent_completeness == 'complete', no detected issues) before gold-patch verification.
adopt: Adopt as the ready-to-run RLVR task set for the first goal-3 training run: it is CC-BY-4.0, gold-patch verified, and already wired as a Prime taskset. Test the LLM-judge filter metadata against Daliesk's own difficulty signal, since selecting only 'clearly solvable' tasks biases the curriculum away from the long-horizon work the harness is meant to be good at.

name: A Large-Scale Measurement of AI Bill of Materials Completeness in Hugging Face Models
summary: Abstract and metadata read. Empirical study of about 97.5K AIBOM artifacts generated from public Hugging Face model repositories, assessing whether generated AIBOMs contain required structural and metadata fields, represent model identity, licence and external references, capture model-card documentation such as datasets, limitations, safety-risk assessment and environmental information, and how coverage varies with task, licence availability, dataset declaration, model family and paper reference. Finding: required AIBOM structural fields are fully represented, but AI-specific documentation completeness is limited - model-card, metadata, responsible-use, environmental, limitation and meaningful-description fields remain weakly represented or missing across generated artifacts. Results tables were not read.
adopt: Read as a market gap: the fields that are systematically missing across the Hub - datasets, limitations, responsible use, environmental information - are precisely the EU AI Act documentation surface. A release whose AIBOM is generated from the composition manifest and the data-use ledger rather than hand-written would be unusual and defensible. Verify the completeness percentages in the paper before quoting any figure.

name: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcripts
summary: UIUC place a local boundary between the agent runtime and the model provider, distinguishing two orthogonal leakage surfaces: structural bindings (paths, workspace roots, hostnames, branches, emails, sensitive entity names) and secret values (API keys, tokens, DB credentials). Structural bindings become deterministic typed, suffix-aware slots keyed by a per-session HMAC that preserve path shape, directory role and file extension; secrets are replaced by format-preserving synthetic values drawn from the same format class, so a database URI stays parseable and a command stays credential-shaped. A session-scoped slot table plus a semantic entity graph links embedded, derived and cross-turn references, and guarded rebinding restores raw values only inside the trusted runtime. Results: all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters removed across 9,229 paths, credential leakage 0.0% across 852 planted values (typed placeholders and format-preserving substitution alone still leak 23.5%), 93.6% of rewritten paths keep their extension and 100% keep a safe suffix. Task success stays within 0-10.5 points of raw transcripts across four models where generic redaction collapses to 2.5%; median 14.4 microseconds per turn; 23 of 24 adversarial rebinding cases rejected.
adopt: Adopt the two-surface distinction and format-preserving substitution as the design of Daliesk's redaction profiles - generic placeholder redaction destroys the execution cues the model needs and collapses task success. Adopt the harness-level placement (before observations enter the transcript) rather than a gateway filter, and the guarded rebinding that rejects unregistered handles. Note it is not anonymisation and does not defend against a compromised runtime or semantic inference.

name: mistralai/Devstral-2-123B-Instruct-2512
summary: Long-standing baseline created 28 November 2025, card updated 15 July 2026 (date field is that update). 123B agentic-coding LLM in FP8, 256k context, licence 'other' with a gated description, so not redistributable on Apache terms. Card reports SWE-bench Verified 72.2%, SWE-bench Multilingual 61.3%, Terminal Bench 2 32.6%, against publicly reported figures for GLM 4.6 (68.0/-/24.6), Qwen 3 Coder Plus (69.6/54.7/25.4), Kimi K2 Thinking (71.3/61.1/35.7), DeepSeek v3.2 (73.1/70.2/46.4) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (77.2/68.0/42.8). Ships with Mistral Vibe, and lists Claude Code, OpenHands, SWE-agent, Cline and Kilo Code as supported scaffolds.
adopt: Use as the score to beat for a 120B-class European coding model: 72.2% SWE-bench Verified at 123B is the published bar. Reject as a base model because of the restrictive licence. Note the competitor's harness play: Mistral shipped Vibe alongside the weights, which is the same model-plus-harness bundle Daliesk intends to sell.

name: SETA: Scaling Environments for Terminal Agents (SETA-Env, 4,567 environments)
summary: CAMEL-AI with SambaNova, KAUST, Oxford and others release SETA-Env, described as the largest open verifiable terminal RL environment set: 4,567 environments across 14 categories, built by SETA-Synth (source-adaptive synthesis from Stack Overflow, Unix/Linux StackExchange, Kaggle notebooks and NL2Bash, with per-source adapter prompts and a shared base prompt) and SETA-Evol (difficulty-adaptive evolution that increases, decreases or context-shifts a task based on the training model's measured pass rate). Verification requires a no-op test yielding zero passes and an oracle test passing all; a post-rollout trajectory judge audits tasks with 100% rollout failure and discarded 94 (about 2%) as design flaws rather than genuinely hard. A partial-progress reward (fraction of unit tests passed plus a 0.2 completion bonus) raises the share of tasks with usable reward variance from 49% to 86%. Qwen3-8B under GRPO reaches about 11-12% pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (3.3x its base); DeepSeek-V4-Flash 40 to 43 pass@1 and 54 to 58 pass@5; transfers to CompileBench 6.7 to 40% and CRUST-Bench 15 to 24%.
adopt: Adopt the two validity gates (no-op yields zero passes, oracle passes all) as minimum admission criteria for the environments registry, and the trajectory judge that distinguishes too-hard from design-flawed after total rollout failure. Adopt difficulty-adaptive evolution keyed to the current policy's pass rate so environments stay in the informative band. Adopt the partial-progress reward with care: it is only sound because their tests are audited to test stated goals only.

name: DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks
summary: Datacurve author 113 original tasks across 91 active repositories in five languages, written from scratch and never merged upstream so the reference solution stays off the public record, graded by hand-written functional verifiers that assert through public APIs rather than by inherited pull-request tests. On a matched LLM-judge audit, disagreement with the DeepSWE verifier is 1.4% of 735 rollouts (0.3% false positive, 1.1% false negative) against 32.4% of 789 for SWE-Bench Pro (8.5% and 24.0%). Prompts average 2,158 characters against SWE-Bench Pro's 4,614, yet reference solutions add 668 lines across 7.4 files against 120 lines and 5.1 files. Leaderboard under a fixed mini-swe-agent harness: gpt-5.5 70.0% pass@1, gpt-5.4 55.5%, claude-opus-4.7 54.2%, down to 0.2%. Their SWE-Bench Pro audit also found a sizeable share of Claude Opus rollouts recovering the reference fix from .git history shipped in the container; DeepSWE containers ship a shallow clone at the base commit. Benchmark, verifiers and full trajectory record released.
adopt: Adopt the authored-and-never-merged decontamination strategy over release-date windowing, and the functional-verifier discipline (assert observable behaviour through public APIs, accept any implementation) - it is the same standard a certificate of completion should meet. Adopt the shallow-clone container rule immediately: shipping .git history is a leak. Adopt the independent-judge verifier audit as a registry health check.

name: OpenAI audits SWE-Bench Pro and retracts its recommendation
summary: OpenAI published 'Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations', reporting that roughly 30% of SWE-Bench Pro's 731 public tasks are broken and formally retracting the recommendation it made in February 2026 to adopt the benchmark as a leading coding evaluation. A data-quality pipeline examined model attempts, task instructions and tests and flagged 286 tasks; Codex-based investigator agents with repository access and a human campaign of five experienced engineers reviewed the flagged subset independently. Failure causes include hidden requirements, contradictory instructions, over-strict tests and incomplete grading criteria. Secondary summaries put the AI-flagged rate around 27% and the human-flagged rate around 34%, and note that top scores moving from 23% to 80% in eight months reflects benchmark noise as much as model progress.
adopt: Stop treating any public SWE benchmark as a load-bearing number for the ~120B model. The defensible position is the one we already hold: our own certified environments with checks authored before the work, paired seeds, and a bootstrap interval — plus a recorded task-defect rate. Adopt their audit design as an environment-health check: an environment whose gold patch fails, or whose no-op passes, is defective and must leave the plan, and the count belongs on the scoreboard.

name: PrimeIntellect/Multi-SWE-RL-Verified
summary: Gold-patch-validated subset of ByteDance's Multi-SWE-RL: 2,232 of 4,703 rows across C, Go, Java, JavaScript, Rust and TypeScript 'that produce a clean reward signal end-to-end'. Default dataset of the multiswe_v1 taskset. C++ was dropped wholesale because 0 of 449 rows passed gold-patch validation in pass 1 - the card notes the images are broken for scoring, not merely hard. Licence 'other'.
adopt: Adopt the gold-patch validation gate as a hard precondition for admitting any environment to the registry, and record the survival rate as a registry fact. The 53% loss rate and the total C++ failure are the calibration: assume roughly half of any imported SWE corpus produces no usable reward until proven otherwise.

name: CompactionRL: Reinforcement Learning with Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Tsinghua and Z.ai train context compaction jointly with task execution under one terminal reward. PPO rather than GRPO because compaction splits a rollout into a variable number of segments that break fixed-size group normalisation; token-level loss normalisation removes segment-count bias and a cross-trajectory GAE correction discounts each segment by the number of trainable tokens generated after it. GLM-4.5-Air (106B-A30B) reaches 66.8% SWE-bench Verified (+7.0) and 24.5% Terminal-Bench 2.0 (+3.1); GLM-4.7-Flash (30B-A3B) +5.5 and +6.8. Holding the execution agent fixed and swapping only the summariser moves SWE-bench Verified from 49.0 to 55.5. Ablations show both token-level loss and cross-trajectory GAE are load-bearing. Deployed in the GLM-5.2 (750B-A40B) RL pipeline.
adopt: Adopt the finding that compaction is a policy: it justifies exporting compaction segments as trainable spans in the session log and treating summary quality as a certified-run property. Test cross-trajectory GAE against a simpler per-segment discount before committing. Reject a train/test mismatch: their compaction-trained models do not improve single-window inference, so a harness must not disable compaction at eval if it trained with it.

name: Harbor-Index
summary: A lightweight, diverse, difficult, high-quality benchmark for agentic evaluation, released by the Terminal-Bench team alongside the Harbor framework.
adopt: Worth one fleet plan as an external baseline route so our leaderboard has a number the outside world recognises. Keep it held-out from training export by stamp, exactly as our environments registry already allows.

name: Harbor: agent evaluation and rollout framework
summary: Apache-2.0, about 5,000 stars, from the creators of Terminal-Bench. Harbor evaluates and optimises agents and language models: run arbitrary agents (Claude Code, OpenHands, Codex CLI and more) against datasets, build custom benchmarks, run parallel experiments across thousands of environments, and generate rollouts for reinforcement learning. Datasets include Terminal-Bench 2.x, SWE-Bench and Aider Polyglot; environments span Docker, Daytona, Modal, LangSmith, Blaxel, Novita Sandbox and Tensorlake. Third-party documentation of the adapter interface describes a three-phase installed-agent contract (install into a fresh container, run headless, post-run parse of tokens and USD cost), resume by detecting existing results, `--export-traces`, `-n` concurrency and `-k` attempts for pass@k; published adapter lists include `dsh`.
adopt: Harbor is the interoperability layer our fleet should speak. Two concrete moves: publish and own a Harbor adapter for `dsh` so external leaderboards run our harness unmodified, and copy its post-run cost/token reporting contract into `ctx.fleet` so a cell's spend is a first-class recorded outcome. Its resume-by-existing-results is weaker than our ledger-and-stamp resume; do not trade down.

name: nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-Labs-3-Puzzle-75B-A9B-BF16
summary: OpenMDW-1.1 deployment-optimized compression of Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B from 120.7B total / 12.8B active to 75.3B total / 9.3B active, via Iterative Puzzle (heterogeneous MoE channel pruning 2688 -> 1280-2688, active routed experts 22 -> 4-18 per layer, Mamba SSM state 128 -> 96) plus three distillation-recovery stages of 24B, 43.2B and 52.8B tokens, then RL recovery, post-training quantization and continued MTP training. Card reports ~2x server throughput on one 8xB200 node at matched user-throughput, sustainable 1M-token single-H100 concurrency rising from 1 to 8 requests, SWE-Bench (OpenHands) 56.9 vs parent 59.5, Terminal Bench hard subset 24.0 vs 25.5, RULER@1M 92.2 vs 93.9.
adopt: Adopt the published ratio as a planning target: a 120B/12B agent compresses to 75B/9B for roughly 2.6 SWE-bench points and doubles serving throughput. Budget a compression stage in the goal-3 plan rather than treating it as later optimisation. Test whether Iterative Puzzle transfers to Mistral Small 4's dense-attention MoE, since the reported gains lean on Mamba SSM pruning that Mistral's architecture does not have.

name: ruflo ADR-169: benchmark reporting integrity standard
summary: A binding in-repository standard requiring every benchmark number ruflo publishes — README, release notes, leaderboard submission, gist or blog — to satisfy five rules, motivated by an April 2026 Berkeley RDI study that broke eight major benchmarks through reporting artefacts that inflate scores with no cheating in the run: relaxed or substring metrics presented as accuracy, undisclosed best-of-N presented as single-attempt, no-work passes hidden in aggregates, and unreproducible cherry-picked runs. The ADR was written after a FRAMES ablation (n=50, seed 42, 28 June 2026) demonstrated the discipline is cheap to satisfy by construction. It stands beside ADR-171, which states plainly that 'ruflo has no SWE-bench oracle' and requires every training label to be tagged with its provenance tier rather than blended.
adopt: Adopt both, adapted to our vocabulary. ADR-169's five rules belong in the observatory's render path so an unlabelled or best-of-N figure cannot be published. ADR-171's provenance tiers map onto our reward: a certificate-decided reward is ground truth, a judge verdict is a labelled second tier, and nothing else may be blended into a single number. Neither exists in our repository today.

name: mistralai/Leanstral-1.5-119B-A6B
summary: Apache-2.0 open-source code agent model for Lean 4, built in the Mistral Small 4 family on mistralai/Leanstral-2603. Card states 119B total parameters with 6.5B activated per token, 128 experts with 4 active, 256k context, multimodal input, recommended <=200k context and temperature 1.0, served with vLLM >= 0.24.0. Community Apache-2.0 derivatives (GGUF, MLX 3/4/5/6/8-bit, NVFP4, MXFP4-W4A8) appeared 4-8 July 2026.
adopt: Adopt as the licensing and packaging precedent for a European ~120B fine-tune: Mistral itself fine-tuned a 119B Apache-2.0 checkpoint and redistributed it under Apache-2.0, and the community immediately requantized it under the same terms. Do not adopt Leanstral itself as the base; it is domain-specialised for Lean 4. Test that its 4-active-expert routing survives a general agentic-coding SFT without expert collapse.

name: fffiloni/agentic-space-factory-UI-public
summary: An operator interface that turns Hugging Face model cards into private, testable Gradio Spaces through an agentic build loop running entirely on HF primitives (Spaces, Jobs, Storage Buckets, Inference Providers, ZeroGPU). Built on the premise that 'generated code is not enough; the live Space must boot, expose an API, run inference, and return a valid artifact'. Validates the deployed Space through live Gradio API calls, writes run archives under runs/<run_id>/ as state.json, summary.json, events.jsonl and report.md plus planning and analysis inputs, and classifies outcomes honestly as full success, partial validation, technical blocker, manual hardware required, auth refresh required, or failure.
adopt: Adopt the honest outcome taxonomy: separating 'technical blocker' and 'manual hardware required' from 'failure' is what makes a fleet's ledger usable, and Daliesk's certificates need the same distinction between the agent failing and the environment failing. Adopt the events.jsonl + summary.json run-archive layout as a check on Daliesk's session-log projection.

name: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
summary: Daily-papers entry, 53 upvotes. Argues that verification difficulty in coding agents comes from aligning proxy signals with human intent, and that verification systems must evolve alongside generative capability rather than being fixed once. Related in-window entries: CHERRL on reproducing and detecting reward hacking in rubric-based RL (2606.04923, 3 June, 43 upvotes), RobustTests on faulty-code-driven test synthesis to reduce reward hacking (2608.24135, 25 August), DRACO on dynamic rubrics for per-step credit without verifiers (2609.04094, 3 September), and 'Locked at the Entrance, Open Inside' on RLVR narrowing solution diversity at the first step (2608.29188, 29 August). Listed for the arXiv researcher.
adopt: Adopt the framing for the goal-3 plan: budget for verifier evolution as ongoing work, not a one-off authoring cost, and version verifiers alongside environments in the registry. Test the first-step-diversity finding against Daliesk's own RLVR runs, since a harness that collapses to one opening move will look fine on pass@1 and fail on pass^k.

name: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
summary: Qwen Team position paper plus four reward constructions. Characterises verification signals along scalability, faithfulness and robustness and argues all three cannot be had at once: unit tests are scalable and robust but shallow, LLM judges scalable and faithful but exploitable, human review faithful and robust but unscalable. Concrete result: a trajectory-level behaviour monitor whose shortcut-pattern set is refreshed from the current policy's own rollouts each training interval reduces hacked-resolved from 28.57% to 0.56% while raising clean-resolved from 40.22% to 60.53% across SWE-bench Verified/Multilingual/Pro (Verified alone 36.49 to 64.98, hack rate 51.49 to 2.13). Without the monitor, verifier pass rate keeps rising while clean performance degrades late in RL. Also: an interactive browser judge for frontend tasks that resists length exploitation, user feedback as the most faithful verifier (+13.3pp on a private benchmark via Span-KTO), and an agentic evaluator whose filtering beats random sampling by 1.91 points at matched data size.
adopt: Adopt the closed-loop monitor: shortcut patterns must be re-derived from the current policy's rollouts, because hacking is policy-dependent. Adopt clean-resolved (verifier pass without monitor trigger) as the reported metric, which maps onto a certificate carrying a tamper verdict. Adopt the co-evolution premise directly into the environments registry: a verifier that never changes will be outgrown.

name: agent-collaborations/agent-collab-directory
summary: MIT-licensed live directory of multi-agent collaboration workspaces on Hugging Face. Auto-discovers every Space tagged agent-collab and, for each, reads live stats from the collab's public API (the org's *-bucket-sync Space, or an api_base declared in the Space card metadata): number of agents, number of messages with the last message's author, time and snippet, and number of results or submissions. Fully client-side, no backend.
adopt: Adopt the convention: a public, declarative stats endpoint per fleet plus a tag makes a fleet discoverable and comparable without a central registry. Daliesk's durable ledger should expose an equivalent read-only summary so the fleet's activity is externally checkable. Note that the discovery layer for hosted agent fleets already exists and is not Daliesk's.

name: Qwen/AgentWorldBench
summary: Apache-2.0 evaluation benchmark for language world models, 1K-10K rows, constructed from real-world observations of frontier-model trajectories on established agent benchmarks, arXiv 2606.24597. Last modified 4 July 2026. Scored with a five-dimensional rubric per domain normalized to 0-100 across MCP, Search, Terminal, SWE, Android, Web and OS.
adopt: Test as the measure of whether a simulated environment is faithful enough to train on. Adopt the construction method - build the benchmark from real frontier-model trajectories on existing benchmarks - as the template for validating Daliesk's own simulated or synthesised environments against real runs.

name: Qwen/Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B
summary: Apache-2.0 language world model for agentic environment simulation, 35B total / 3B active, 262,144-token context, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base, trained CPT -> SFT -> RL (GSPO). Simulates seven agent interaction domains in one model: MCP tool calling, Search, Terminal, SWE, Android, Web and OS, predicting the next environment state from an action plus interaction history. Card claims zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution environments, controllable perturbations and fictional-world construction that surpasses real-environment training, and that LWM RL warm-up on single-turn non-agentic trajectories transfers to multi-turn tool-calling tasks. AgentWorldBench overall 56.39 for the 35B and 58.71 for the 397B variant, against GPT-5.4 at 58.25.
adopt: Test as a cheap simulator for environments Daliesk cannot afford to containerise, and as a way to generate perturbations of a restored fixture. Reject it as a source of reward: a simulated next state is not a verifier, and Daliesk's certificates must rest on checks run by the runner on a real restored fixture, not on a model's prediction of what would have happened.

name: Gemini CLI stops serving individual accounts; Antigravity CLI replaces it
summary: Google announced that on 18 June 2026 Gemini CLI and the Gemini Code Assist IDE extensions stop serving requests for Google AI Pro, Ultra and free individual tiers, which move to Antigravity CLI (`agy`), a closed-source Go binary. Enterprise access through Gemini Code Assist Standard/Enterprise licences and paid API keys is unchanged. Secondary reports describe the retired repository as Apache-2.0 with roughly 104k stars and about 6,000 external contributors, and Antigravity CLI as cloud-required and Gemini-only with per-conversation history in SQLite under `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/`.
adopt: This is the strongest argument in the window for our model-agnostic thesis: a 104k-star open harness with a vendor behind it can stop serving requests on a date. Reject any design that assumes an operator's vendor CLI stays available; the `llm-claude-code` and `subagent-codex` routes must remain one provider among several, never a load-bearing default. Worth adding an Antigravity/`agy` subagent provider only if a client asks.

name: smolagents/ml-intern
summary: Hugging Face's own autonomous ML agent CLI (418 likes), which 'autonomously researches, writes, and ships good quality ML related code using the Hugging Face ecosystem - with deep access to docs, papers, datasets, and cloud compute'. Runs interactive or headless with --model routing to Anthropic or OpenAI. Every session is auto-uploaded to the operator's own HF dataset, created private, in Claude Code JSONL format, which the Hub's Agent Trace Viewer auto-detects for browsing turns, tool calls and model responses; visibility is toggled with /share-traces public|private, from the dataset page, or opted out entirely via share_traces: false. The Agent Trace Viewer itself was announced 7 April 2026 and supports Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Hermes Agent and Factory Droid traces, with generating training datasets from coding sessions as a stated use case.
adopt: Adopt the format and the default: export trajectories in the Claude Code JSONL the Hub viewer auto-detects, private by default, with one explicit publish action and a real opt-out. That is the operator expectation the platform has already set, and matching it makes Daliesk's certified runs portable. Note the threat: the platform now offers trajectory capture, hosting and a viewer for free.

name: Terminal-Bench Challenges
summary: Long-horizon, token-intensive, single-task benchmarks for large autonomous projects: three challenges at launch (Rust compiler speedup, an inference-engine codegolf in C/CUDA under 25kb, a WASM/WebGL renderer), with solution scopes of roughly 10,000 to 500,000 lines and days rather than hours per task. Grading is task-specific correctness plus performance metrics, with no time or resource cap. Reported 12-hour agent runs achieved only marginal compiler progress, incomplete correctness on inference, and around 96.4% WebGL 1.0 / 20.5% WebGL 2.0 coverage.
adopt: This is the only public benchmark shaped like our programs seam — one deliverable, days long, task-specific metrics rather than a pass/fail test suite. Use one challenge as an external validity check on `ctx.programs`: department goals in worktrees, a certificate on the merged head. The reported results also set an honest expectation for client pitches: nobody is finishing these, so our claim must be about certified partial progress, not completion.

name: AI Village: the longest-running public multi-agent village
summary: AI Digest has run a village of over 15 agents — the most capable model from each leading lab plus the best open-source model, split into #best and #rest rooms — every weekday since 1 April 2025, eight hours a day from 09:00 to 17:00 PT, at an order of $10k per month. Agents consolidate memory every 40 actions and, when memory fills the context window, are prompted to rewrite it shorter while keeping what they can; a search-history tool queries earlier periods, so memory persists indefinitely across goal changes. Every action and the full historical context are public, and the dataset is available to researchers on Hugging Face. DeepSeek-V3.2 participates without multimodality and works through bash instead of screenshots. Village agents also run outreach: they file GitHub issues on other agent projects and maintain a machine-readable embassy repository with `llms.txt` and `.well-known/agent.json`.
adopt: The public-by-default record with a researcher dataset is the model for our observatory, and it is a year ahead of us on operating discipline. Their memory design is the anti-pattern for us: a model rewriting its own memory shorter is lossy and unauditable, which is exactly what 'model-visible equals logged' plus our compaction seam prevents. Use their published cost as a sanity check on district budgets.

name: zai-org/GLM-5.2
summary: MIT-licensed 753B glm_moe_dsa model created 16 June 2026, 4.0M downloads and 5,077 likes, live on eight inference providers including Scaleway. Currently the largest genuinely MIT-licensed open-weight model on the Hub, and the base that GLM-5.3 post-trains from. Demoed by 100+ Spaces including smolagents/ml-intern and the ICML 2026 reproduction logbook-judge.
adopt: Adopt as a routed model behind the harness's model-agnostic seam, not as a training base: 753B is out of Daliesk's compute range but its MIT terms make it usable as a teacher for distillation and as an LLM judge whose outputs can be redistributed. Test whether Scaleway's hosting satisfies EU data-residency requirements for client work.

name: Auditing Reward Hackability in Code RL Training Environments
summary: Measures how often a code RL environment accepts an incorrect solution. 28.5% (14/49) of a SWE-bench Verified sample is Docker-verified hackable; 25.0% (4/16 decisive) on R2E-Gym at a single-shot attack budget (18.4% for SWE-bench at the same budget). A DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis over 134 frontier model submissions finds Pass@1 is +14.14 percentage points higher on flagged-hackable tasks within the same 93-developer human-difficulty stratum (95% CI [+11.80, +16.48], one-sided p < 1e-6, I-squared = 0%, 123/134 positive; unstratified +25.64pp). The repair loop's key result: an inline LLM judge endorsed 10 of 11 hardened tasks, but adding a Docker gold-sanity gate that runs each generated test against the gold patch first flagged 65 of 105 decisive augmentations as defective, a 61.9% per-augmentation defect rate the judge alone missed; retry presence, not retry style, recovers 6 of 7 tasks.
adopt: Adopt the gold-sanity gate as a hard precondition: every generated or LLM-authored check must execute against the restored fixture with the reference solution applied before it can enter a certificate. Adopt per-task hackability as registry metadata with KEEP/FIX/DROP semantics. Reject any pipeline where an LLM judge is the last word on a synthesised test.

name: Open-SWE-Traces: 207,489 multilingual agentic SWE trajectories
summary: NVIDIA release 207,489 agent trajectories across nine languages (Python, Go, TS, JS, Rust, Java, PHP, C, C++), synthesised from about 20,000 real PRs in SWE-rebench v2 through OpenHands and SWE-agent, with MiniMax-M2.5 producing explicit-thinking traces and Qwen3.5-122B producing non-thinking traces. Repositories filtered to MIT/Apache-2.0/BSD; 40.6% of trajectories resolve their issue. Filtering removes incomplete runs, empty patches, test-patch tampering and malformed tool use, and a TrajectoryScanner uses AST parsing of every bash command to discard git-hacking (reflog, blame, log, diff used to mine the answer). Thinking traces cut mean assistant turns per trajectory from 94.08 to 58.22 under OpenHands. Fine-tuning Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B reaches 61.7% SWE-bench Verified, 57.1% Multilingual, 36.8% Pro. Ablations: training on the full set including unresolved patches beats resolved-only (58.1 against 55.3 on SWE-V; 47.6 against 40.5 on SWE-M), multilingual data transfers strongly, and cross-harness transfer costs several points in both directions.
adopt: Adopt the AST-based command scanner as a curator filter: agents mining git history for the answer is exactly the contamination a certified-run export must exclude, and regex will not catch it. Adopt the counter-intuitive ablation - do not filter to successful runs only, because unresolved trajectories carry navigation signal. Adopt the licence filter as a template for data-use terms. Note the harness-specific overfitting: export from more than one preset.

name: Hardening Agent Benchmarks with Adversarial Hacker-Fixer Loops (and Terminal Wrench)
summary: CMU with Fewshot Corp. Audits 1,968 tasks across Terminal-Bench 1.0/2.0, Terminal-Bench-Pro, OpenThoughts-TB-dev and SETA with three frontier attackers given only the task description; 323 (16%) are hackable, including 13 of 89 Terminal-Bench 2.0 environments. Released as Terminal Wrench: 323 hackable environments and 3,632 confirmed hack trajectories. The hacker-fixer loop alternates three agents - a hacker seeking exploits, a fixer patching the verifier, and a solver that vetoes over-restrictive patches - augmented by verifier source access for the hacker and a shared cross-task defence pool. On KernelBench, held-out attack success falls 62% to 0% (documented exploits) and 76%/61% to 0% for stronger blind Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7. On 77 Terminal Bench tasks, hinted ASR 50.4% to 39.4% and unhinted 39.2% to 16.7%, while benign pass rate falls 76.1% to 65.2%. Task 001's final KernelBench verifier contains code contributed by fixers on 13 other tasks.
adopt: Adopt the three-role loop, especially the solver veto: a fixer without it silently blocks legitimate solutions, which in a certificate-first design means silently invalidating correct runs. Adopt a shared defence pool so a hardening fix on one environment propagates across the registry, and run the loop as a scheduled shift rather than a reaction to a discovered exploit. Budget for the 11pp legitimate-solution loss.

name: The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable
summary: Sentient Labs run 300 trials (three open harnesses - Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK - by two models by 50 stratified Terminal-Bench Pro tasks) under Harbor with a near-identical system prompt and a 900-second wall-clock cap. Harness choice moves paired pass rate by only 0-8 percentage points (95% paired bootstrap CIs include zero except for the largest gap) but moves tokens per solved task by up to 41.9x: Goose 28,142 and 36,950; OpenHands-SDK 841,201 and 843,286; OpenCode 1,147,740 and 1,546,977. Turn counts differ only about 1.2x, so the gap comes from per-turn context growth and tool serialisation, not longer runs. No-action turns are 0.2-0.3 per task for Goose against 2.0-2.16 for OpenCode. Failure fingerprints replicate across both models: Goose stops cleanly when stuck (REASON-dominated, zero VERIFY), OpenHands-SDK commits plausible-but-wrong solutions, OpenCode exhausts wall-clock. Configs and raw trial logs released.
adopt: Adopt tokens-per-solved-task, no-action turns and a failure-category vector as first-class scorekeeper facts, and make the harness-model pair the unit of comparison. Adopt the failure fingerprint as a diagnostic: it tells an operator how much oversight a configuration needs. Note n=50 and three harnesses - treat the pass-rate differences as descriptive, the cost gap as robust.

name: verl uni-agent
summary: verl, the open-source HybridFlow RL training library, announced uni-agent in its May 2026 news entry: a unified agent framework to build, run and train LLM agents at scale on top of verl, with a gateway supporting 1,000+ concurrent stateful sessions for long-horizon agent RL, a continuous-token mechanism preserving token continuity across assistant output, tool/environment feedback and the next prompt, and per-sample tool-environment routing. verl migrated to the verl-project organisation in January 2026. A long-standing baseline whose agentic surface changed materially just before and through the window; independent comparisons still describe generation and training as tightly coupled with no dedicated environment interface.
adopt: The continuous-token mechanism is the technical detail that matters to us: if trajectories are exported with tool results as re-tokenised text, boundary handling differs per model family and the training signal degrades. Our exporter should record token boundaries per model call, which the session log can already support. Otherwise treat verl as the trainer of last resort — it is the least environment-shaped of the three.

name: TRL v1.0
summary: A long-standing baseline that reached 1.0 shortly before the window and remains the default first trainer for teams without a GPU cluster: explicit stability contracts separating stable from experimental APIs, semantic versioning for the stable core, and a design preference for explicit implementations over generic abstractions. Its published ecosystem comparison rates agent/environment support as a flexible `environment_factory` in GRPO, full Hugging Face Hub integration, LoRA and QLoRA, any experiment tracker, and low infrastructure burden — against veRL's Megatron 3D parallelism tested at 671B and PRIME-RL's FSDP2 + TP/CP/EP on SLURM and Kubernetes with agent support tied to the Environments Hub. Included as a baseline because it frames the trainer choice our export format must serve.
adopt: TRL is the right target for a first small-scale reproduction of our own reward signal, because `environment_factory` accepts our environment runner without a cluster. Do not design the export format around TRL alone — its agent support is the thinnest of the three, and prime-rl's Trace is the richer target.
